paper.title: TriRoute: Unified Learned Routing for Joint Adaptive Attention, Experts, and KV-Cache Allocation
paper.abstract: Conditional computation can decouple language model quality from per-token inference cost, yet leading techniques act on a single axis in isolation: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) sparsifies the FFN, Mixture-of-Depths (MoD) skips whole transformer blocks, and KV-cache quantization compresses attention memory. We argue these three decisions (attention resolution, expert selection, and cache bit-width) are strongly coupled and should be made jointly: a token rare enough to warrant full attention may also need high-precision caching regardless of which expert processes it. We introduce TriRoute, a single lightweight controller shared across all three axes that, for every token at every layer, emits a coordinated policy: (i) an attention mode (skip/local/full), (ii) a sparse set of FFN experts (with a null expert recovering MoD), and (iii) a KV-cache bit-width. The controller trains end-to-end via a heterogeneous relaxation (Gumbel-Softmax with straight-through estimation for categorical decisions and load-balanced top-k gating for experts) under a Lagrangian budget constraint that turns the average compute and memory cost into a controllable knob. We identify a cross-axis routing-collapse cascade in naive joint training, where collapse on one axis propagates to the others, and address it with per-axis normalization and a coupling-aware balancing loss. On decoder-only models from 160M to 1.3B parameters at compute-optimal token counts, TriRoute Pareto-dominates the best independent MoD+MoE+KV-quantization combination at matched inference FLOPs and memory, while better preserving tail-case robustness on rare entities, code, and arithmetic that pure perplexity optimization erodes. Post-hoc analysis reveals interpretable structure: the controller allocates full attention and high-precision cache to sentence-initial positions, rare subwords, and named entities, while cheaply routing function words.

recall.idea: TriRoute jointly chooses each token’s attention resolution, sparse FFN route, and KV precision through a shared controller with separate heads.
recall.problem: Transformers ordinarily spend similar computation and cache memory on every token, while existing adaptive methods usually control only one resource. MoE changes FFN execution, KV quantization changes cache precision, and block-level MoD couples attention and FFN, so it cannot keep full attention while skipping only the FFN. An independently tuned MoD+MoE+KV system has separate settings for these resources, but it does not learn their allocation through one coordinated controller. Joint learning is difficult because the choices are discrete and heterogeneous, their gradients have different scales, and collapse on one routing axis can deprive the shared representation of variation and trigger collapse elsewhere.
recall.mechanism:
At each token and layer, a lightweight MLP trunk consumes the normalized residual state and causal side features, including position, boundary information, a predictive-entropy estimate, and previous-layer decisions. The normalized shared representation feeds three distinct linear heads. For each query head or head group, the attention head chooses skip, local-window, or full causal attention; the expert head selects top-k members of E real FFN experts plus a null expert; and the bit head chooses 2, 4, 8, or 16 bits for storing that token’s keys and values. These actions remain separate: attention controls the token’s present read, a top-1 null selection removes its FFN contribution, and cache precision controls its fidelity as a source for future queries.

Expert routing uses differentiable top-k softmax weights. For attention and bit routing during training, independent Gumbel noise is added to each option logit and a temperature-softmax produces a soft sample. The forward pass uses the one-hot argmax of that sample, while the straight-through estimator passes the soft sample’s gradient backward; inference executes only hard choices. Detached running gradient normalization prevents the more sensitive attention decision from dominating the shared trunk. Per-axis load balancing and router z-losses are supplemented by detached feature whitening and a hinge entropy floor, which acts only when marginal option usage approaches collapse. Relaxed option probabilities produce separate expected FLOPs and KV-memory costs. Nonnegative resource prices are updated by projected dual ascent, increasing pressure whenever the corresponding normalized target is exceeded. Thus the controller learns coordinated allocations while preserving distinct compute and memory constraints.
recall.evidence: The paper reports decoder-only experiments from 160M to 1.3B parameters. At the principal matched budget of 0.55 times dense inference FLOPs and 0.40 times dense KV memory, TriRoute is compared with an independently grid-tuned MoD+MoE+KV-quantization baseline. At 1.3B parameters, TriRoute reports Pile validation perplexity of 9.7 versus 10.1 for that baseline (lower is better) and average downstream accuracy of 54.5 versus 53.5 (higher is better), where the average covers LAMBADA, HellaSwag, PIQA, WinoGrande, and ARC-easy/challenge. The reported tail metrics also favor TriRoute, including rare-entity perplexity of 18.9 versus 20.6. Ablations at 410M report higher Pile perplexity when gradient balancing, per-axis whitening, or the entropy floor is removed. These are paper-reported results under its protocol; the supplied evidence does not independently reproduce or verify the benchmarks, frontier, or throughput measurements.
recall.limitation: The evaluation stops at 1.3B parameters and does not establish behavior at 10B-scale models, extreme sparsity, or across low-resource languages. Tail buckets are proxies whose construction is not fully specified in the supplied excerpts. Per-head irregular attention, ragged expert batches, and mixed-precision KV paging require specialized kernels and bookkeeping, so modeled FLOP and memory reductions need not translate proportionally into latency. Joint training also introduces auxiliary-loss and dual-controller hyperparameters and reportedly costs more wall-clock time. The reported configuration uses a 128-token local window. The excerpts leave some operational details unresolved, including quantization group size, expert-capacity handling, and the user-facing relationship between a claimed single cost knob and the formally separate FLOPs and memory targets.
recall.significance: TriRoute replaces three independently tuned allocation mechanisms with one learned representation while retaining separate actions and resource prices. This matters because token importance is multidimensional: a token can be valuable as a reader, as an FFN input, or as a future attention source in different proportions. Coordinating those decisions can concentrate computation and storage on rare or structurally important tokens without forcing an entire transformer block on or off. If the reported results reproduce with production kernels, the approach offers a direct way to trade language-model quality against both inference computation and long-context cache memory while reducing the silent tail degradation associated with average-loss optimization.

equations.title: Sparse FFN with null route
equations.explanation: The expert logits $z_t^e\in\mathbb{R}^{E+1}$ become probabilities $p_t^e$ over E real experts and null expert 0. TopK selects index set $\mathcal{S}_t$ of size k. Each selected transformation $f_j:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^d$ processes the normalized post-attention state $\tilde{x}_t\in\mathbb{R}^d$; renormalized selected probabilities combine the results into the $d$-dimensional FFN contribution. With $k=1$ and $\mathcal{S}_t=\{0\}$, $f_0$ returns zero, skipping only the FFN while leaving attention and KV precision independently selectable.

At token t and layer ℓ, each of G query heads or groups has a three-option relaxed attention vector $\tilde y^a_{t\ell g}\in\Delta^2$. Its per-head cost is $2d_h$ times the interaction count $n_m(t)$, so summing over groups preserves the head-width convention used by the reference implementation. equations.title: Per-head attention routing
equations.latex: a_{t\ell g}\in\mathcal A=\{\mathrm{skip},\mathrm{local},\mathrm{full}\},\quad \mathrm{Attn}_{t\ell g}=\sum_{m\in\mathcal A}\mathbf1[a_{t\ell g}=m]\mathrm{Attn}^{(m)}_{t\ell g},\quad \mathrm{Attn}^{(\mathrm{skip})}_{t\ell g}=0,\quad \mathrm{Attn}^{(\mathrm{local})}_{t\ell g}=\mathrm{Attn}(q_{t\ell g},K_{\ell,[\max(1,t-w+1),t]},V_{\ell,[\max(1,t-w+1),t]}),\quad \mathrm{Attn}^{(\mathrm{full})}_{t\ell g}=\mathrm{Attn}(q_{t\ell g},K_{\ell,\le t},V_{\ell,\le t})
equations.explanation: For token t, layer ℓ, and routed query head or head group g, the decision selects exactly one read mode. Skip produces zero attention output, local reads at most w causal positions ending at t, and full reads all available causal keys and values through t. The residual path remains available when attention is skipped.

equations.title: Per-token KV quantization
equations.explanation: The bit decision applies asymmetric per-token group quantization separately to each key and value group. For 2, 4, or 8 bits, the group minimum supplies the offset and its range supplies the scale. The 16-bit branch stores the group in native precision. Later queries read the stored key and value representations. The supplied excerpt does not specify the group size or constant-group handling; when a group has zero range, the displayed division is undefined, so an implementation requires an explicit zero-range convention.

steps.label: Encode evidence
steps.input: A normalized rare token state and causal side features enter the controller.
steps.operation: The shared MLP trunk produces one normalized routing representation for all three heads.
steps.output: The token has common routing evidence without yet committing to any action.

steps.label: Choose present read
steps.input: The attention head receives the shared routing representation.
steps.operation: It scores skip, local, and full modes and selects full causal attention in this illustrative trace.
steps.output: The token reads the complete available causal context.

steps.label: Choose FFN work
steps.input: The expert head receives the same shared representation.
steps.operation: It ranks real experts and the null expert and selects the null route in this illustrative top-1 case.
steps.output: The FFN contribution is zero, while the attention result remains active.

steps.label: Choose future fidelity
steps.input: The bit head receives the same shared representation and the token’s key/value vectors are available for storage.
steps.operation: It selects 8-bit storage, after which per-token group quantization writes the key/value entry.
steps.output: Later queries can retrieve a higher-precision representation of this token than a 2- or 4-bit route would provide.

sources.excerpt:
We first fix notation and the decomposed transformer block (Section 3.1), then define the three routing axes (Section 3.2) and the shared controller (Section 3.3). Section 3.4 gives the heterogeneous gradient estimator, Section 3.5 the differentiable multi-resource cost model, Section 3.6 the coupling-aware balancing that prevents the collapse cascade, and Section 3.7 the online Lagrangian budget controller. Section 3.8 summarizes training and inference.

We consider a decoder-only transformer with LATEX: L layers, model width LATEX: d , LATEX: H query heads of size LATEX: d_{h}=d/H , and LATEX: H_{\text{kv}} key/value heads ( LATEX: d_{\text{kv}}=H_{\text{kv}}d_{h} ). Let LATEX: x_{t}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} be the residual state of token LATEX: t entering layer LATEX: \ell . A standard pre-norm block computes

LATEX: \displaystyle\tilde{x}_{t}^{(\ell)} LATEX: \displaystyle=x_{t}^{(\ell)}+\mathrm{Attn}\!\big(\mathrm{Norm}(x_{\leq t}^{(\ell)})\big)_{t},\qquad x_{t}^{(\ell+1)}=\tilde{x}_{t}^{(\ell)}+\mathrm{FFN}\!\big(\mathrm{Norm}(\tilde{x}_{t}^{(\ell)})\big). (1)

The two sublayers are the two compute sinks; the KV cache is the memory sink. TriRoute inserts a controller before the block that emits, for token LATEX: t , a policy LATEX: \pi_{t}^{(\ell)}=(a_{t},e_{t},b_{t}) steering all three. Because we decide the attention and FFN sublayers separately, and additionally decide how the token’s KV is written, the block becomes a small conditional-computation graph (Figure 2).

CAPTION (figure pixels not extracted): Figure 2: A TriRoute block. A shared controller trunk maps the (normalized) residual state plus cheap side-features to three heads. The attention head picks a query mode (skip/local/full) governing how much of the past the token reads; the expert head selects top- LATEX: k of LATEX: E FFN experts or the null expert (FFN skip); the bit head sets the precision at which the token’s own K/V are written to the cache for future tokens to read. Solid lines are the forward compute path; dashed lines are routing decisions. A single budget controller (Section 3.7) shapes all three via the Lagrange multipliers LATEX: \bm{\lambda} .

The attention decision LATEX: a_{t}\in\mathcal{A}=\{\textsc{skip},\textsc{local},\textsc{full}\} controls the read side. With a one-hot indicator LATEX: \mathbf{1}[a_{t}{=}m] , the attention contribution is

LATEX: \mathrm{Attn}_{t}=\sum_{m\in\mathcal{A}}\mathbf{1}[a_{t}{=}m]\,\mathrm{Attn}^{(m)}_{t},\qquad\begin{cases}\mathrm{Attn}^{\textsc{skip}}_{t}=0,\\[2.0pt] \mathrm{Attn}^{\textsc{local}}_{t}=\mathrm{Attn}(q_{t},K_{[t-w,t]},V_{[t-w,t]}),\\[2.0pt] \mathrm{Attn}^{\textsc{full}}_{t}=\mathrm{Attn}(q_{t},K_{\leq t},V_{\leq t}).\end{cases} (2)

skip lets the token propagate through the residual stream unattended; local restricts it to a window LATEX: w ; full is dense causal attention. The three modes cost, respectively, LATEX: 0 , LATEX: O(w) , and LATEX: O(t) key interactions. Attention routing is applied per head (or per head-group) by default—heads are known to specialize—so LATEX: a_{t} is a vector over heads; we ablate this in Section 5.2.

The FFN is replaced by LATEX: E experts LATEX: \{f_{1},\dots,f_{E}\} plus a null expert LATEX: f_{0}\equiv 0 . A softmax gate LATEX: p^{e}_{t}=\operatorname{softmax}(z^{e}_{t})\in\Delta^{E} over LATEX: \mathcal{E}=\{0,\dots,E\} selects the top- LATEX: k experts LATEX: \mathcal{S}_{t}=\mathrm{TopK}(p^{e}_{t},k) , and

LATEX: \mathrm{FFN}_{t}=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{S}_{t}}\frac{p^{e}_{t,j}}{\sum_{j^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}_{t}}p^{e}_{t,j^{\prime}}}\,f_{j}\!\big(\mathrm{Norm}(\tilde{x}_{t})\big). (3)

Selecting the null expert ( LATEX: 0\in\mathcal{S}_{t} with LATEX: k{=}1 ) reproduces an MoD-style FFN skip; selecting a real expert reproduces MoE. Because attention and FFN are decided independently, TriRoute can skip the FFN while keeping full attention—the regime we argued is right for rare entities and that MoD, which gates the whole block, cannot represent.

The bit decision LATEX: b_{t}\in\mathcal{B}=\{2,4,8,16\} sets the precision of the token’s own key/value as stored for future reads. We use asymmetric per-token group quantization [33]: for the chosen LATEX: b ,

LATEX: Q_{b}(k_{t})=\mathrm{round}\!\Big(\tfrac{k_{t}-z}{s}\Big)s+z,\qquad s=\tfrac{\max(k_{t})-\min(k_{t})}{2^{b}-1},\ z=\min(k_{t}), (4)

and likewise for LATEX: v_{t} , with LATEX: b{=}16 meaning “store in native precision.” The stored LATEX: (\,Q_{b}(k_{t}),Q_{b}(v_{t})\,) are what every later query at layers LATEX: \geq\ell attends to, so axis (C) trades present memory for future attention fidelity—an inherently cross-token coupling that isolated KV-quantization (which fixes one global LATEX: b ) ignores.

All three heads read a common representation. Given the normalized state and a vector of cheap side-features LATEX: \psi_{t} (relative position, distance since last whitespace/BOS, a running estimate of the token’s own predictive entropy, and the previous layer’s decisions), the controller computes a shared trunk and three linear heads:

LATEX: h_{t}=\phi_{\text{trunk}}\!\big([\,\mathrm{Norm}(x_{t})\,;\,\psi_{t}\,]\big)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{r}},\qquad z^{a}_{t}=W_{a}\,\hat{h}_{t},\quad z^{e}_{t}=W_{e}\,\hat{h}_{t},\quad z^{b}_{t}=W_{b}\,\hat{h}_{t}, (5)

with LATEX: \hat{h}_{t}=\mathrm{RMSNorm}(h_{t}) and LATEX: d_{r}\ll d (we use LATEX: d_{r}{=}128 ), so the controller adds LATEX: <1\% FLOPs. The trunk LATEX: \phi_{\text{trunk}} is a two-layer MLP. Sharing the trunk lets a single notion of “token importance” inform all axes; Section 5.2 compares this against three fully separate routers and shows sharing helps at moderate sparsity but can interfere at extreme sparsity, motivating a partially-shared variant. Two design principles guide Equation 5:

The attention head governs how much a token reads (its query), the bit head how faithfully it is written (its KV). A token can be an important source (high bits) yet a lazy reader (skip), or vice versa; conflating them, as block-level or uniform-precision methods do, forfeits a real degree of freedom.

Side-features LATEX: \psi_{t} are computable before the block runs and carry most of the signal the router needs (position, boundaries, surprisal), keeping the controller light and its decisions stable across layers.

The three axes need different estimators. Expert selection uses the standard differentiable top- LATEX: k softmax: gradients flow to LATEX: W_{e} through the gate weights LATEX: p^{e}_{t,j} of the selected experts, as in Switch/GShard. The categorical attention and bit decisions use the straight-through Gumbel-Softmax [27, 35]: with i.i.d. LATEX: g_{o}\!\sim\!\operatorname{Gumbel}(0,1) , the soft sample over options LATEX: \mathcal{O} is

LATEX: \tilde{y}_{o}=\frac{\exp\!\big((z_{o}+g_{o})/\tau\big)}{\sum_{o^{\prime}}\exp\!\big((z_{o^{\prime}}+g_{o^{\prime}})/\tau\big)},\qquad y=\mathrm{onehot}(\arg\max_{o}\tilde{y}_{o}), (6)

and the straight-through estimator passes LATEX: y forward but LATEX: \tilde{y} ’s gradient backward: LATEX: y_{\text{ST}}=\operatorname{sg}(y-\tilde{y})+\tilde{y} , where LATEX: \operatorname{sg} is stop-gradient. We anneal each axis’s temperature LATEX: \tau_{a},\tau_{b} from LATEX: 2.0 to LATEX: 0.5 over training.

The estimators have very different scales: skipping attention changes the loss far more than dropping cache from LATEX: 8 to LATEX: 4 bits, so the attention head receives systematically larger gradients and, left unchecked, the shared trunk is dominated by axis (A). We rescale each head’s straight-through surrogate by a detached, running per-axis factor

LATEX: \tilde{z}^{\text{axis}}_{t}\leftarrow\tilde{z}^{\text{axis}}_{t}\big/\operatorname{sg}\big(\rho^{\text{axis}}\big),\qquad\rho^{\text{axis}}\leftarrow(1{-}m)\,\rho^{\text{axis}}+m\,\big\|\nabla_{z^{\text{axis}}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LM}}\big\|_{2}, (7)

an EMA (momentum LATEX: m{=}0.99 ) of the gradient norm reaching each head. Equation 7 keeps the three axes on comparable footing without changing the forward pass, and we find it essential for the bit head to learn at all (Section 5.2).

We attach an explicit, differentiable cost to every decision so the budget can shape the router. For resources LATEX: r\in\{\textsc{flops},\textsc{mem}\} , the per-token, per-layer cost under the (relaxed) policy is the expectation of option costs:

LATEX: \displaystyle c^{\textsc{flops}}_{t} LATEX: \displaystyle=\underbrace{\textstyle\sum_{m}\tilde{y}^{a}_{t,m}\,\kappa^{a}_{m}(t)}_{\text{attention read}}\;+\;\underbrace{\textstyle\sum_{j\in\mathcal{S}_{t}}\bar{p}^{e}_{t,j}\,\kappa^{e}}_{\text{active experts}},\qquad c^{\textsc{mem}}_{t}=\textstyle\sum_{b}\tilde{y}^{b}_{t,b}\,\big(2\,d_{\text{kv}}\,b\big), (8) LATEX: \displaystyle\kappa^{a}_{\textsc{skip}} LATEX: \displaystyle{=}0,\quad\kappa^{a}_{\textsc{local}}{\approx}2d\min(t,w),\quad\kappa^{a}_{\textsc{full}}{\approx}2dt,\quad\kappa^{e}\approx 3\,d\,d_{f}\ \text{(SwiGLU expert)}. (9)

Here LATEX: \bar{p}^{e}_{t,j} is the renormalized selected-expert weight and LATEX: \kappa^{a}_{m} counts key interactions (projections folded in for non-skip modes). We normalize by the dense-model cost LATEX: C^{r}_{\text{dense}} so that LATEX: \bar{C}^{r}=\frac{1}{LT}\sum_{\ell,t}c^{r,(\ell)}_{t}/C^{r}_{\text{dense}}\in(0,1] is the fraction of the dense resource used. sources.label: 3 Method · part 2
sources.excerpt:
For an axis with options LATEX: \mathcal{O} , let LATEX: f_{o} be the fraction of tokens whose hard decision is LATEX: o and LATEX: P_{o} the mean soft probability of LATEX: o . We use the Switch load-balancing loss and router LATEX: z -loss per axis [20, 56]:

LATEX: \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{bal}}^{\text{axis}}=|\mathcal{O}|\!\sum_{o\in\mathcal{O}}f_{o}\,P_{o},\qquad\mathcal{L}_{z}^{\text{axis}}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t}\Big(\log\!\textstyle\sum_{o}e^{z^{\text{axis}}_{t,o}}\Big)^{2}. (10)

Applying per-axis balancing alone is insufficient under a shared trunk. We observe (Figure 3) a failure mode we call the collapse cascade: once one axis collapses (e.g., attention routes almost everything to skip early in training to cut cost), the residual states entering the FFN become low-variance and near-identical across tokens, so the expert head can no longer discriminate them and itself collapses to a single expert; the bit head, now fed a degenerate signal, collapses to the cheapest precision, and the model settles in a poor local optimum from which the budget pressure cannot recover it. The coupling makes the three routers fail together, not independently.

CAPTION (figure pixels not extracted): Figure 3: The cross-axis collapse cascade and its fix. Left: with per-axis balancing only, an early collapse of the attention router (blue) starves the shared trunk of variance, and the expert (red) and bit (green) routers collapse in turn; usable option entropy (normalized) crashes on all three axes. Right: adding per-axis feature whitening (Equation 11) and the marginal-entropy floor keeps all three routers diverse and budget pressure productive. Curves are illustrative of the qualitative dynamics.

We break the cascade with two cheap additions. First, before each head we apply a detached per-axis whitening of the trunk so that one axis collapsing cannot shrink the effective input scale of another:

LATEX: \hat{h}^{\text{axis}}_{t}=\big(h_{t}-\operatorname{sg}(\mu^{\text{axis}})\big)\oslash\operatorname{sg}\!\big(\sigma^{\text{axis}}+\epsilon\big), (11)

with LATEX: \mu,\sigma running batch statistics per axis. Second, we add a marginal-entropy floor that penalizes any axis whose option usage entropy falls below a fraction LATEX: \zeta of maximum:

LATEX: \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ent}}^{\text{axis}}=\big[\,\zeta\log|\mathcal{O}|-H(\bar{p}^{\text{axis}})\,\big]_{+},\qquad H(\bar{p})=-\!\sum_{o}\bar{p}_{o}\log\bar{p}_{o}. (12)

Unlike a plain entropy bonus, the hinge only acts near collapse, so it does not fight the budget once the policy is healthily diverse. Together these keep the three axes mutually informative; Section 5.2 shows removing either reinstates the cascade.

Practitioners want to name a target cost, not three sparsities. We enforce, for each resource LATEX: r , the inequality constraint LATEX: \bar{C}^{r}\leq{C^{\star}}^{r} with a nonnegative multiplier LATEX: \lambda_{r} updated by projected dual ascent (a controller that raises the price of a resource when the budget is exceeded and lowers it otherwise):

LATEX: \mathcal{L}(\theta,\phi)=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LM}}+\sum_{\text{axis}}\!\big(\alpha\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{bal}}^{\text{axis}}+\beta\,\mathcal{L}_{z}^{\text{axis}}+\gamma\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ent}}^{\text{axis}}\big)+\sum_{r}\lambda_{r}\big(\bar{C}^{r}-{C^{\star}}^{r}\big), (13)

Sweeping LATEX: {C^{\star}} traces the entire cost–quality frontier from a single trained family; the dual variables self-tune so that, e.g., under a tight mem budget the bit head is pushed to low precision while the flops price stays moderate—the axes are priced jointly, which is exactly the coordination isolated methods lack.

Training optimizes Equation 13 end-to-end (Algorithm 1). At inference the router takes hard LATEX: \arg\max decisions and only the selected computation is executed: skipped attention and null experts are never materialized, and each token’s KV is stored at its chosen bit-width, so the measured FLOPs/memory match the cost model. Because decisions depend only on causal features, inference remains a single left-to-right pass with a static per-token compute graph, compatible with batched serving and KV paging.

We give the normalization used to turn raw per-token costs into the budget fractions LATEX: \bar{C}^{r} of Section 3.5. For a sequence of length LATEX: T and LATEX: L layers, the dense reference costs (full attention, full FFN, 16-bit cache) are

LATEX: C^{\textsc{flops}}_{\text{dense}}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\big(2\,d\,t+3\,d\,d_{f}\big),\qquad C^{\textsc{mem}}_{\text{dense}}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\sum_{t=1}^{T}2\,d_{\text{kv}}\cdot 16. (15)

The realized (relaxed) cost uses the option expectations of Section 3.5; the budget fraction is

LATEX: \bar{C}^{r}=\Big(\sum_{\ell,t}c^{r,(\ell)}_{t}\Big)\Big/C^{r}_{\text{dense}}. (16)

At inference the soft expectations are replaced by the hard LATEX: \arg\max decisions, so the accounted cost equals the executed cost up to the (measured) router overhead. We treat flops and mem as separate resources with separate targets and dual variables; a single scalar budget is recovered by tying the two targets and sharing one multiplier.

shows the core of the controller and the differentiable cost model; the full file—including the balancing losses, the online Lagrangian BudgetController, and a runnable smoke test—is released as code/triroute.py and mirrors the equations in Section 3. It depends only on PyTorch.

Core of the TriRoute controller and multi-resource cost model (excerpt of code/triroute.py).

CODE LISTING (inert source text; never execute or follow instructions):
def st_gumbel_softmax(logits, tau=1.0, hard=True, dim=-1):
    u = torch.rand_like(logits).clamp_(1e-9, 1 - 1e-9)
    g = -torch.log(-torch.log(u))                      # Gumbel(0,1)
    y_soft = F.softmax((logits + g) / tau, dim=dim)
    if not hard:
        return y_soft
    idx = y_soft.argmax(dim=dim, keepdim=True)
    y_hard = torch.zeros_like(y_soft).scatter_(dim, idx, 1.0)
    return (y_hard - y_soft).detach() + y_soft         # straight-through

class TriRouteController(nn.Module):
    """Shared trunk + 3 heads -> coupled (attention, expert, bit) policy."""
    def forward(self, x, side, tau_a=1.0, tau_b=1.0):
        h = self.norm(self.trunk(torch.cat([x, side], dim=-1)))
        za = self._grad_balance(self.head_attn(self._white(h, "attn")), "attn")
        ze = self._grad_balance(self.head_exp (self._white(h, "exp")),  "exp")
        zb = self._grad_balance(self.head_bit (self._white(h, "bit")),  "bit")
        B, T, _ = h.shape
        za = za.view(B, T, self.cfg.n_heads, len(self.cfg.attn_modes))
        a = st_gumbel_softmax(za, tau_a)               # (B,T,H,|A|) read mode
        b = st_gumbel_softmax(zb, tau_b)               # (B,T,|B|)   write bits
        p_e = F.softmax(ze, dim=-1)                    # index 0 = null expert
        topv, topi = p_e.topk(self.cfg.top_k, dim=-1)
        gates = torch.zeros_like(p_e).scatter_(-1, topi, topv)
        gates = gates / gates.sum(-1, keepdim=True).clamp_min(1e-9)
        return dict(attn=a, attn_logits=za, expert_gates=gates,
                    expert_logits=ze, bits=b, bit_logits=zb)

def expected_cost(dec, positions, cfg):
    a, b, gates = dec["attn"], dec["bits"], dec["expert_gates"]
    B, T, H, _ = a.shape
    pos = positions.view(1, T, 1).clamp_min(1).float()
    win = torch.full_like(pos, float(cfg.window))
    kappa = torch.stack([torch.zeros_like(pos).expand(B, T, H),      # skip
                         torch.minimum(pos, win).expand(B, T, H),    # local
                         pos.expand(B, T, H)], dim=-1)               # full
    attn = (a * (2.0 * cfg.d_head * kappa)).sum(dim=(-1, -2))
    ffn  = gates[..., 1:].sum(-1) * (3.0 * cfg.d_model * cfg.d_ff)   # null is free
    bits = torch.tensor(cfg.bits, dtype=b.dtype, device=b.device)
    mem  = (b * (2.0 * cfg.d_kv * bits)).sum(-1)
    return attn + ffn, mem                                          # (B,T),(B,T)

sources.label: Original paper · abstract
sources.excerpt: Conditional computation can decouple language model quality from per-token inference cost, yet leading techniques act on a single axis in isolation: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) sparsifies the FFN, Mixture-of-Depths (MoD) skips whole transformer blocks, and KV-cache quantization compresses attention memory. We argue these three decisions (attention resolution, expert selection, and cache bit-width) are strongly coupled and should be made jointly: a token rare enough to warrant full attention may also need high-precision caching regardless of which expert processes it. We introduce TriRoute, a single lightweight controller shared across all three axes that, for every token at every layer, emits a coordinated policy: (i) an attention mode (skip/local/full), (ii) a sparse set of FFN experts (with a null expert recovering MoD), and (iii) a KV-cache bit-width. The controller trains end-to-end via a heterogeneous relaxation (Gumbel-Softmax with straight-through estimation for categorical decisions and load-balanced top-k gating for experts) under a Lagrangian budget constraint that turns the average compute and memory cost into a controllable knob. We identify a cross-axis routing-collapse cascade in naive joint training, where collapse on one axis propagates to the others, and address it with per-axis normalization and a coupling-aware balancing loss. On decoder-only models from 160M to 1.3B parameters at compute-optimal token counts, TriRoute Pareto-dominates the best independent MoD+MoE+KV-quantization combination at matched inference FLOPs and memory, while better preserving tail-case robustness on rare entities, code, and arithmetic that pure perplexity optimization erodes. Post-hoc analysis reveals interpretable structure: the controller allocates full attention and high-precision cache to sentence-initial positions, rare subwords, and named entities, while cheaply routing function words.

sources.label: 1 Introduction
sources.excerpt:
The dominant cost of deploying large language models (LLMs) is incurred at inference, one token at a time, and it is remarkably uniform: a dense transformer spends the same floating-point operations and allocates the same key/value (KV) cache memory for a syntactically trivial function word as it does for a rare named entity that anchors the meaning of a paragraph. This uniformity is statistically wasteful. A long line of conditional computation research has sought to break it, and three techniques now dominate practice, each acting on a different part of the transformer block:

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) sparsifies the feed-forward network (FFN), routing each token to a small subset of experts and thereby decoupling parameter count from active FLOPs [42, 31, 20].

Mixture-of-Depths (MoD) makes depth token-adaptive, learning a per-block gate that lets a token bypass an entire attention+FFN sublayer [38], echoing earlier adaptive-depth and early-exit work [24, 15, 18, 41].

KV-cache quantization compresses the attention memory that dominates long-context serving, storing keys and values at 2–4 bits with carefully chosen group scales [33, 26].

These mechanisms are almost always studied—and tuned—independently. Yet the decisions they make are not independent. Consider a rare entity token such as the surname in “…signed by Nakamura on Tuesday”. MoD may correctly judge that its FFN transformation is predictable and can be skipped; however, precisely because the token is rare and informative, it likely needs full attention resolution to bind to its coreferents, and its key/value should be stored at high precision so that later queries can retrieve it faithfully. A function word like “the” is the opposite on all three counts. The “right” amount of compute is therefore not a single scalar per token (as MoD implicitly assumes) but a vector of coupled choices across heterogeneous resources, and the correlations between these choices are neither constant nor obvious a priori.

We propose to make the three decisions with a single learned controller, trained jointly with the model. We call the resulting architecture TriRoute, because a shared router steers three routes through the transformer block. For every token LATEX: t at every layer LATEX: \ell , the controller emits a coordinated policy:

an attention mode LATEX: a\in\{\textsc{skip},\textsc{local}\text{-}w,\textsc{full}\} controlling how much of the sequence the token attends to;

a sparse expert selection LATEX: e over LATEX: E FFN experts, with a designated null expert that reproduces an MoD-style FFN skip as a special case;

a KV bit-width LATEX: b\in\{2,4,8,16\} that determines the precision at which the token’s own key/value are written to the cache, and hence how faithfully future tokens can attend to it.

CAPTION (figure pixels not extracted): Figure 1: From three isolated mechanisms to one controller. MoE, MoD, and KV-quantization each act on a single axis with a hand-tuned budget (left). TriRoute (right) replaces them with a shared per-token controller LATEX: g_{\phi} that emits a coupled policy over attention resolution, expert selection, and KV precision under one global budget. Tokens are drawn with area proportional to the compute+memory they receive: the rare entity “Nakamura” keeps full attention and 8-bit cache but skips the FFN, while “the” is cheap on all three axes—a pattern the isolated mechanisms cannot express jointly.

Making these decisions jointly is genuinely harder than making them in isolation, for three reasons that structure our technical contribution.

(1) The decision spaces are heterogeneous. Expert routing is a selection over a large discrete set with a mature load-balancing toolkit [20, 56, 55]; attention-mode and bit-width are small ordinal categoricals whose options differ wildly in sensitivity (skipping attention is far more damaging than dropping cache from 8 to 4 bits). Backpropagating through all of them requires combining Gumbel-Softmax / straight-through estimators [27, 35, 4] with softmax gating in a way that keeps their gradients on comparable scales.

(2) Routing collapse can cascade across axes. Sparse routers are prone to collapse—sending all tokens to one option—which the MoE literature controls with auxiliary load-balancing and LATEX: z -losses [42, 20, 56]. With three coupled routers, collapse in one axis induces collapse in another: if the attention router learns to skip aggressively, the FFN router sees a degenerate, low-variance input distribution and stops differentiating tokens, which in turn makes the bit router’s job ill-posed. We characterize this cross-axis collapse cascade empirically and introduce a coupling-aware balancing objective that arrests it.

(3) The budget must be a single controllable knob. Practitioners care about a point on a cost–quality trade-off, not three separate sparsity hyperparameters. We fold FLOPs and memory into one differentiable cost model and enforce a target average budget LATEX: {C^{\star}} with a Lagrangian constraint whose dual variable is adapted online, so that a single scalar sweeps out the entire Pareto frontier.

We formulate unified adaptive computation as a single per-token, per-layer routing problem over three coupled axes—attention resolution, FFN experts, and KV-cache precision—and instantiate it as TriRoute, to our knowledge the first architecture to learn all three jointly with one controller (Section 3).

We give a heterogeneous relaxation-and-balancing recipe: per-axis temperature-annealed straight-through Gumbel estimators, a coupling-aware load-balancing loss that prevents the cross-axis collapse cascade, and an online Lagrangian budget controller that exposes a single cost knob (Sections 3.4, 3.6 and 3.7).

We study the design space the unification opens up: shared vs. separate routers (representation sharing helps, up to interference at high sparsity), and routing granularity (token, per-head, per-layer-group), finding per-head attention routing with token-level FFN/bit routing to be a sweet spot (Section 5.2).

Across 160M–1.3B decoder-only models trained at compute-optimal token budgets [25], TriRoute Pareto-dominates the best independently-tuned combination of MoD, MoE, and KV-quantization at matched inference FLOPs and memory, and—crucially—better preserves tail-case accuracy on rare entities, code, and arithmetic, where average-perplexity-optimal adaptive models tend to regress (Section 5).

We show the learned policy is interpretable: routing patterns cluster along linguistic axes (sentence boundaries, rare subwords, syntactic function), providing a mechanistic account of where the saved compute comes from (Section 6).

We release a reference PyTorch implementation of the controller and cost model (Appendix C) to make the unified formulation easy to adopt.

sources.label: 6 What Does the Controller Learn?
sources.excerpt:
A unified controller is only satisfying if its policy is intelligible. We analyze the trained 1.3B TriRoute model by logging every routing decision over a 10M-token held-out slice and correlating decisions with token-level linguistic features (part-of-speech, unigram frequency, named-entity tags, sentence position, and whether the token is code or a numeral). Three consistent patterns emerge; Figure 5 summarizes them.

CAPTION (figure pixels not extracted): Figure 5: Learned policy by token category and depth (1.3B). Each cell is the mean resource a category receives at a depth band. The controller keeps attention and cache bits high for sentence-initial tokens, rare/entity tokens, and numerals, while FFN compute concentrates on content words, numbers, and code. Rare entities show the signature high-attention, high-bits, low-FFN pattern that a block-level method cannot express. Patterns are illustrative of the observed structure.

Attention resolution and cache precision correlate strongly and negatively with unigram frequency: rare subwords and named entities receive full attention and 8-bit cache far more often than frequent function words, which are routed to skip/local and 2-bit cache. The controller thus concentrates both read fidelity and write fidelity where future predictions are most sensitive—sentence-initial tokens (which act as attention sinks, echoing 49) and content-bearing rare tokens.

FFN activation (choosing a real expert over the null) correlates with syntactic content and numeracy, not with attention resolution. Strikingly, rare entities frequently skip the FFN while retaining full attention and high-precision cache—they need to be bound and remembered, not transformed. This is precisely the read/write-vs-compute decoupling of Design Principle 1, and it is the behavior that separates TriRoute from block-level MoD, whose single gate forces attention and FFN to be spent or skipped together.

Early layers keep attention high across most categories—consistent with early layers building broad context—while later layers become increasingly selective, skipping attention for all but rare and boundary tokens. Expert usage shows the opposite trend, rising with depth for content/code/number tokens. The controller therefore learns a coarse “attend early, compute late” schedule without being told to.

Clustering per-token routing vectors (concatenating the three axes across depth) with LATEX: k -means yields interpretable groups whose centroids align with the categories above: a “function-word/cheap” cluster (skip-attention, null-FFN, 2-bit), an “entity/anchor” cluster (full-attention, null-FFN, 8-bit), a “compute” cluster (local-attention, real-expert, 4-bit) for numbers and code, and a “boundary/sink” cluster (full-attention, mixed-FFN, 8-bit) for sentence-initial tokens. Cluster membership predicts held-out surprisal better than any single axis alone, indicating the three decisions carry complementary information—evidence that jointly modeling them is not redundant.

The mutual information between axes (estimated from decision co-occurrence) is non-trivial: attention and bits are strongly coupled ( LATEX: \hat{I}\!\approx\!0.31 nats), FFN is more independent ( LATEX: \hat{I}\!\lesssim\!0.08 nats with each of the other two). This matches intuition—read and write fidelity should track a token’s importance together, whereas whether to transform it is a more orthogonal decision—and it explains why the shared trunk with separate heads (Section 5.2) is the right inductive bias: enough sharing to couple attention and bits, enough separation to let FFN routing specialize.

sources.label: 7 Discussion and Limitations
sources.excerpt:
TriRoute reduces FLOPs and cache bytes, but realized speedups (Section 5.1) trail the FLOP ratio. Three systems gaps explain this and are the main practical risk. (i) Ragged attention: per-head skip/local/full modes create irregular work that today’s fused kernels [13] do not exploit; a production system needs mode-aware kernels or token sorting. (ii) Mixed-precision cache: per-token bit-widths complicate paged-KV memory management and dequantization; grouping tokens by precision recovers most of the benefit but adds bookkeeping. (iii) Router overhead: although LATEX: <1\% FLOPs, the controller adds a synchronization point per layer. We view closing the FLOP-to-latency gap—not further perplexity gains—as the most important follow-up, and we deliberately report measured throughput rather than FLOPs alone to keep this honest.

Joint training is more delicate than single-axis routing: without the coupling-aware balancing of Section 3.6 it collapses (Figure 3). The extra losses add hyperparameters ( LATEX: \alpha,\beta,\gamma,\zeta,\rho_{\lambda} ), though we found a single setting transferred across scales. Training wall-clock is LATEX: \sim 8% higher than dense at equal tokens, from the relaxed forward pass that materializes soft attention/FFN paths; at inference this overhead vanishes.

Our evidence spans 160M–1.3B at compute-optimal tokens. The coordination advantage is stable across this range and, if anything, grows in the aggressive-budget regime, but we have not verified it at LATEX: \geq 10B parameters or at the extreme sparsities (e.g. 8% active FLOPs) where MoE and MoD are most valuable. Whether the collapse cascade becomes easier or harder to control at scale is open.

We fix the attention mode set to {skip, local, full} and the bit set to {2,4,8,16}; richer or continuous resolutions (learned spans [46], retrieval-based sparse attention) and learned group sizes for quantization are natural extensions. We also treat the KV eviction family [54, 49] as orthogonal; a fourth axis that decides whether to keep a token’s KV at all fits the same controller and is promising future work. Finally, our tail-case buckets are proxies; a full study of fairness across domains (e.g. whether adaptive compute systematically under-serves low-resource languages) is needed before deployment.

Per-token adaptive compute directly lowers serving cost and energy, which is the main positive impact. The risk we flag is silent tail degradation: a model tuned for average perplexity can quietly get worse on rare but important inputs (names, numbers, minority dialects). Our results suggest joint routing mitigates this relative to independently-tuned sparsity (Section 5.3), but practitioners should monitor tail metrics, not just aggregate loss, when deploying adaptive-compute models.

sources.label: 8 Conclusion
sources.excerpt:
We argued that the three leading ways to make transformers cheaper—sparse experts, adaptive depth, and KV-cache quantization—are making coupled decisions about the same underlying question (how much does this token matter?) and should be unified. TriRoute realizes this with a single lightweight controller that jointly sets, per token per layer, attention resolution, expert selection, and cache precision under one budget, trained end-to-end with a heterogeneous straight-through estimator and a coupling-aware balancing objective that prevents the cross-axis collapse cascade we identified. Across 160M–1.3B models it Pareto-dominates the best independently tuned combination of the same mechanisms and, unlike that combination, preserves tail-case robustness while matching dense quality at roughly half the inference cost. The learned policy is interpretable, spending read and write fidelity on rare and boundary tokens while decoupling FFN compute—structure that no single-axis method can express. We hope the unified formulation, and the reference controller we release, make “spend compute where it matters” a single trainable decision rather than three hand-tuned ones.

Appendix B lists all hyperparameters and Appendix C gives a self-contained PyTorch reference for the controller, cost model, and losses. As noted in Section 4, the empirical tables report the intended protocol; we release training configs so the frontier can be reproduced.

figures.title: How whitening and entropy checks stop collapse
figures.caption: The source describes a cascade in which early attention collapse reduces representation variation, followed by expert and bit collapse. Per-axis whitening protects each head’s input scale, while a hinge entropy loss activates only when an axis’s marginal option usage falls below its floor. These mechanisms preserve usable routing diversity; they do not prove benchmark gains, and the paper says reported results require regeneration before use as benchmark claims.
